item.title: My sister-in-law charged me $60 for the "family discount" wedding cake she promised for free. I smiled, paid her, and quietly canceled her catering job for my own wedding...
item.description:
My sister-in-law charged me $60 for the "family discount" wedding cake she promised for free. I smiled, paid her, and quietly canceled her catering job for my own wedding...
I remember the exact moment the card reader beeped. Priya turned it toward me like she was showing off a new phone, and there it was, glowing on the little screen: $60.00. TOTAL DUE.
"It's just for the extra tier stand and the delivery box," she said, not quite looking at me. "I have to charge somebody for that stuff, Odette. Can't just eat the cost every time."
I had the receipt from four months earlier still saved in my email, the one where she wrote, in all caps, "CAKE IS OUR GIFT TO YOU TWO, DON'T EVEN THINK ABOUT PAYING ME." I didn't bring it up. I tapped my card, watched the little green checkmark appear, and said, "No problem. Thank you, Priya."
She smiled like she'd done me a favor.
I smiled back. Then I got in my car, sat in her driveway for exactly four minutes without starting the engine, and opened the contract folder on my phone. Priya's catering business, Petal & Crumb, was booked to cater my entire reception. Sixty-eight guests. Four thousand seven hundred thirty dollars. I had already paid her eleven hundred and eighty dollars as a deposit, back when Wendell and I still thought hiring family was a nice, sentimental idea.
I found the number for a caterer named Marisol Frey, whose food truck had done my office's holiday party the year before, and I texted her before I even pulled out of the driveway: "Are you still taking wedding bookings for October? I might have an opening."
I want to be clear that it wasn't about sixty dollars. Sixty dollars is nothing. It's a tank of gas and a sandwich. What it was about sat heavier in my chest than that, something I hadn't let myself name yet, something that had been building since a dinner four months earlier where Colette, my mother, had made a promise on Priya's behalf that Priya apparently never intended to keep.
My phone buzzed twenty minutes later. Marisol: "I have October 11th open. Let's talk numbers."
I hadn't told Wendell yet. I hadn't told my mother. I definitely hadn't told Priya, who was, at that exact moment, probably already telling someone in her family group chat that she'd "handled the Odette situation."
I didn't answer Marisol right away. I sat with my thumb over the screen, thinking about the deposit I'd already paid, the six weeks I had left before the wedding, and the fact that once I did this, there was no undoing it. Priya would find out. Everyone would find out. And I had absolutely no idea how far she'd go once she did.
I typed back anyway: "Let's talk."
The dinner where this all started was back in June, at my parents' house, the kind of Sunday dinner where somebody always brings up money by accident. Wendell and I had just told everyone the wedding was set for October, and my mother, Colette, had turned to Priya across the table and said, loud enough for the whole room, "Priya's doing the cake. Family rate. Practically free, right, Priya?"
Priya had laughed and said, "Of course. It's Odette's wedding. What kind of sister-in-law charges for that?"
I remember thinking, at the time, that it was a strange thing to promise on someone's behalf without asking them first, but Priya said it herself. She agreed. She even hugged me over the table, knocking my water glass, and said, "I'm doing the whole cake as my gift. No arguing."
Six weeks before the wedding, standing in her driveway with a $60 charge on my card, I thought about that hug a lot.
Priya had started Petal & Crumb about two years earlier, after she left a corporate job in food service management that she never talked about except to say it had "burned her out completely." My brother Desmond was proud of her. Everyone was proud of her. She'd catered my mother's sixtieth birthday, my cousin's baby shower, a handful of things, and each time, something small happened that I brushed off. At my mother's birthday,
